title: De drei schwatten Princessinnen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 137. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 137, told in Low German, is a compressed, almost riddling tale: a besieged town is ransomed by a poor fisherman's son, who is then carried off and stumbles into an enchanted castle where three princesses, black-skinned under a curse and only a little white in the face, need one act of nerve to be freed. The disenchantment and its aftermath come in quick, elliptical strokes — a gallows scene, a return home unrecognized, a final reunion — closer to a folk anecdote's pace than a fairy tale's. Because the dialect is thick and the plot moves fast, this is a good short text to sit with sentence by sentence.

sentences.t: Ostindien was von den Fiend belagert, he wull de Stadt nig verloeten, he wull ersten seshundert Dahler hebben.
sentences.l: East India was besieged by the enemy; he would not leave the town, he wanted first to have six hundred thalers.
sentences.i: East India was under siege by the enemy, and he would not quit the town before he had six hundred thalers.
sentences.n: The whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), Westphalian — narration and all, as KHM 19 and KHM 47 are. Two spellings to fix at once, because they run through every line: was here is war, “was” (the dialect word for “what” is wat), and he is er, “he.” wull = wollte; verloeten = verlassen; ersten is erst, “first, beforehand”; seshundert = sechshundert; Dahler = Taler; hebben = haben. Ostindien, the East Indies, is simply a name from far away hung on a Westphalian village tale.

sentences.t: Do leiten se dat ut trummen, well de schaffen könne, de soll Börgemester weren.
sentences.l: Then let they it be drummed out: whoever could provide them, he should become mayor.
sentences.i: Then they had it cried through the streets by drum: whoever could raise the money should be made mayor.
sentences.n: leiten here is ließen, “let, had something done” — not leiten, “to lead”; and well is wer, “whoever,” not will. “ut trummen” = austrommeln: a town crier walked the streets beating a drum and announcing the news. de picks up the thalers; Börgemester = Bürgermeister; weren = werden. do = da, “then,” and it opens nearly every sentence in this tale.

sentences.t: Do was der en armen Fisker, de fiskede up de See mit sinen Sohn,
sentences.l: Then was there a poor fisherman, who fished on the sea with his son,
sentences.i: Now there was a poor fisherman there, who was out fishing on the sea with his son,
sentences.n: der here is da, “there” — the second there of “da war da ein armer Fischer” — and not the article; the tale uses der for “there” three more times. fiskede = fischte; sinen = seinem. The dialect does not keep the High German case endings apart, so armen stands where the standard language would want armer.

sentences.t: do kam de Fiend un nam den Sohn gefangen un gav em doför seshundert Dahler.
sentences.l: then came the enemy and took the son captive and gave him six hundred thalers for it.
sentences.i: then the enemy came and took the son prisoner, and gave the father six hundred thalers for him.
sentences.n: “gefangen nehmen” is to take prisoner; em = ihm, the father; doför = dafür, in exchange for that. The bargain is stated flatly and never remarked on again: the father sells his son to the besieging army for the price of the town.

sentences.t: Do genk de Vader hen un gav dat de Heerens in de Stadt,
sentences.l: Then went the father off and gave it to the gentlemen in the town,
sentences.i: Then the father went off and gave it to the gentlemen of the town,
sentences.n: genk = ging; hen = hin, “off, thither.” “gav dat de Heerens” puts the person given to in a bare dative with no preposition, exactly as High German does: gab das den Herren. Heerens = Herren, here the town council.

sentences.t: un de Fiend trock av un de Fisker wurde Börgemester.
sentences.l: and the enemy drew off and the fisherman became mayor.
sentences.i: and the enemy marched away, and the fisherman was made mayor.
sentences.n: “trock av” = zog ab, marched off, with av (ab) standing after the verb. The office is won and the son is gone in the same breath, and the tale does not pause over it.

sentences.t: Do word utropen wer nig „Heer Börgemester“ segde, de soll an de Galge richtet weren.
sentences.l: Then was it proclaimed: whoever did not say “Mister Mayor,” he should be executed on the gallows.
sentences.i: Then it was proclaimed that whoever did not say “Mister Mayor” should be hanged.
sentences.n: word = wurde, here the passive auxiliary; utropen = ausgerufen, cried publicly. Heer is Herr, “Mister, sir” — not das Heer, an army; segde = sagte; “richtet weren” = gerichtet werden, to be put to death by sentence, not richten “to set right.” The fisherman’s first act as mayor is to make a wrong form of address a hanging matter.

sentences.t: De sohn de kam de Fiend wier ut de Hände un kam in en grauten Wold up en haujen Berg.
sentences.l: The son, he came out of the enemy’s hands again and came into a great wood, up a high mountain.
sentences.i: The son got out of the enemy’s hands again, and came into a great wood, up on a high mountain.
sentences.n: “de Fiend … ut de Hände” is a bare dative of the person: out of the enemy’s hands. The doubled “De sohn de …” — the subject, then a resuming der — is ordinary spoken emphasis in this dialect and comes again in the next line. wier = wieder; grauten = großen; Wold = Wald; haujen = hohen. The 1857 text prints sohn here with a small letter where it capitalises Sohn elsewhere; that is the source’s own inconsistency, left as it stands.

sentences.t: De Berg de dei sick up,
sentences.l: The mountain, it did itself open,
sentences.i: The mountain opened,
sentences.n: “dei sick up” = tat sich auf: updohn, sich auftun, with the prefix up waiting at the end. dei is tat, the past of tun; sick = sich. A mountain that opens of itself is a fixed piece of German folk tale, and no explanation is offered or expected.

sentences.t: do kam he in en graut verwünsket Schloß, woin Stohle, Diske un Bänke alle schwatt behangen wören.
sentences.l: then came he into a great enchanted castle, wherein chairs, tables and benches were all hung with black.
sentences.i: and he came into a great enchanted castle, where the chairs, the tables and the benches were all hung with black.
sentences.n: verwünsket = verwünscht, enchanted, under a spell. woin = worin; Stohle = Stühle; Diske = Tische; schwatt = schwarz, the word the whole tale turns on. A room hung with black is a room in mourning: the reader is meant to know at once that something here is unreleased.

sentences.t: Do queimen drei Princessinnen, de gans schwatt antrocken wören, de men en lück (wenig) witt in’t Gesicht hädden,
sentences.l: Then came three princesses, who were dressed all in black, who had only lück (a little) white in the face,
sentences.i: Then three princesses came, dressed all in black, with only a little white in the face,
sentences.n: (wenig) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis, printed in the 1857 text to explain the dialect lück to their own readers — eight such brackets stand in this tale, and every one of them is theirs, not an editor’s. Where they gloss a dialect word this way, the literal line keeps the dialect word and puts their gloss, translated, in the brackets — so the reader sees the same help their own readers were given. queimen = kamen; gans = ganz (not die Gans, a goose); antrocken = angezogen; men = nur; witt = weiß; hädden = hatten. The white in the face measures how far the enchantment has been lifted, and the plot turns on it.

sentences.t: de segden to em he soll men nig bange sien, se wullen em nix dohn, he könn eer erlösen.
sentences.l: they said to him he should only not be afraid, they would do him nothing, he could redeem them.
sentences.i: and they told him he need only not be afraid; they would do him no harm, and he could set them free.
sentences.n: segden = sagten; “bange sien” = bange sein, to be afraid; nix = nichts; dohn = tun. könn is könne, the subjunctive of reported speech — “he could,” as they said it. eer here is sie, “them,” where the same word elsewhere in the tale is ihr, “their.” erlösen, to redeem, release, is the standing word for lifting an enchantment and is this tale’s keyword.

sentences.t: Do seg he je dat wull he gern dohn, wann he men wüste wo he dat macken söll.
sentences.l: Then said he yes, that would he gladly do, if he only knew how he was to do it.
sentences.i: Then he said yes, he would do it gladly, if only he knew how it was to be done.
sentences.n: je here is ja, “yes,” not je, “ever”; and seg is sagte, “said” (seggen = sagen) — the commonest verb in the tale, and not sehen. wann = wenn; men = nur; wüste = wüßte; wo here is wie, “how” (this dialect writes wo, wu and wü for it); macken = machen; söll = sollte.

sentences.t: Do segget se he söll en gans Johr nig met en kühren (sprechen), un söll se auck nig anseihen:
sentences.l: Then say they he should a whole year not kühren (speak) with anyone, and should not look at them either:
sentences.i: Then they said he must not speak with anyone for a whole year, and must not look at them either:
sentences.n: (sprechen) is the Grimms’ own gloss for the dialect kühren. segget is the present tense — “they say” — in the middle of a past narrative, which this tale does throughout. “en gans Johr” = ein ganzes Jahr, where the en of “met en kühren” two words later is a different word: it may be einem, “with anyone,” or ihnen, “with them,” and the text does not settle it. auck = auch; anseihen = ansehen. Silence and averted eyes are the usual conditions of a redemption tale — and they are what makes the ending a broken promise, not just a fright.

sentences.t: wat he gern hebben wull, dat söll he men seggen, wann se Antwort giewen dröften (geben dürften), wullen se et dohn.
sentences.l: what he would gladly have, that should he only say; when they an answer giewen dröften (were allowed to give), they would do it.
sentences.i: Whatever he wanted he had only to say; when they were permitted to answer, they would see to it.
sentences.n: (geben dürften) is the Grimms’ own gloss for giewen dröften. dröften = dürften; wullen = wollten. The frame “wat … dat …” — a free relative caught up by dat — is the ordinary German way of putting the object first: was er gern haben wollte, das sollte er nur sagen.

sentences.t: As he ’ne Tied lang der west was, sede he he wull asse gern noh sin Vader gohn,
sentences.l: When he had been there a time long, said he he would then gladly go to his father,
sentences.i: When he had been there a while, he said he would like to go to his father,
sentences.n: As = als; “’ne Tied lang” = eine Zeit lang; der is da, “there,” again; “west was” = gewesen war; sede = sagte. The doubled “sede he he wull” is not a slip — the first he is the subject of “said,” the second of the reported clause. asse in this line is genuinely obscure: everywhere else in the tale it is als, “as, when,” which will not fit here, and it may stand for also, “so, in that case.”

sentences.t: da segget se dat söll he men dohn,
sentences.l: then say they that should he only do,
sentences.i: then they said that he should certainly do,
sentences.n: men (nur) here is not the restricting “only” but the encouraging one — by all means, do it. The princesses raise no objection whatever, which is what makes the advice he gets at home so damaging.

sentences.t: düssen Buel (Beutel) met Geld söll he met niermen, düsse Klöder soll he antrecken, un in acht Dage möst he der wier sien.
sentences.l: this Buel (purse) with money should he take with him, these clothes should he put on, and in eight days must he be there again.
sentences.i: this purse of money he was to take with him, these clothes he was to put on, and in eight days he must be back there.
sentences.n: (Beutel) is the Grimms’ own gloss for the dialect Buel. acht here is the numeral eight, not die Acht, “heed”: in acht Dagen, within eight days. düssen/düsse = diesen/diese; Klöder = Kleider; antrecken = anziehen; “met niermen” = mitnehmen; möst = müßte; der = da, there. Everything is arranged except the year of silence, which nobody mentions again.

sentences.t: Do werd he upnurmen (aufgehoben), un is glik in Ostindien.
sentences.l: Then is he upnurmen (lifted up), and is at once in East India.
sentences.i: Then he was caught up, and at once he was in East India.
sentences.n: (aufgehoben) is the Grimms’ own gloss for the dialect upnurmen — lifted up and carried off, rather than “put away safely,” which is what aufheben more usually means. werd = wird; glik = gleich, at once. The journey itself is simply not told: he is picked up and set down.

sentences.t: Do kann he sin Vader in de Fiskhütte nig mer finden un frög de Luide wo doh de arme Fisker blierwen wöre,
sentences.l: Then can he his father in the fisher-hut no more find, and asked the people where then the poor fisherman had got to,
sentences.i: But he could not find his father in the fisherman’s hut any more, and asked the people what had become of the poor fisherman,
sentences.n: frög = fragte; Luide = Leute; doh = doch, the particle of impatience — where has he got to, then?; “blierwen wöre” = geblieben wäre, and “wo is he blieben?” is the ordinary German for what became of him. mer = mehr. He is asking after a man who is now the mayor, and does not know it.

sentences.t: do segget se dat möst he nig seggen, dann queim he an de Galge.
sentences.l: then say they that he must not say, then would he come to the gallows.
sentences.i: and they told him he must not say that, or he would come to the gallows.
sentences.n: möst = müßte; queim is käme, the subjunctive of consequence — he would come to the gallows. The decree from the first part is hanging over the whole town, and the son walks straight into it.

sentences.t: Do kümmt he bi sin Vader, do seg he „Fisker, wo sin ji do to kummen?“
sentences.l: Then comes he to his father, then says he “fisherman, how are you come to that?”
sentences.i: Then he came to his father and said: “Fisherman, how did you come by all this?”
sentences.n: wo here is wie, “how,” and sin is seid, “are” — the same three letters that mean “his” a few words earlier in sin Vader. ji = ihr, the plural “you” a stranger uses; “do to kummen” = dazu gekommen. And he addresses his father as Fisker — the one word the town may not use.

sentences.t: Do seg de „dat möt ji nig seggen, wann dat de Heerens van de Stadt gewahr weeret, kümme ji an de Galge.“
sentences.l: Then says he “that you must not say; if the gentlemen of the town get wind of it, you come to the gallows.”
sentences.i: Then he said: “You must not say that; if the gentlemen of the town get wind of it, you will come to the gallows.”
sentences.n: de stands here on its own for “he” — the article doing the work of a pronoun, which this dialect does freely. möt = müßt; “gewahr weeret” = gewahr werden, to get wind of; “kümme ji” = kommt ihr. The father warns the son without knowing him.

sentences.t: He willt ober gar nig loten, he werd noh de Galge bracht.
sentences.l: He will however not at all leave off, he is brought to the gallows.
sentences.i: But he would not leave off at all, and he was brought to the gallows.
sentences.n: ober is aber, “but” — nothing to do with Ober-; willt is will, “he wants” (3rd sg.), not “will it”; loten = lassen, here to leave off, to stop; bracht = gebracht. The tale never says why he insists, and leaves the reader to watch a son force his father to look at him.

sentences.t: Es he do is, seg he „o mine Heerens, gierwet mie doh Verlöv dat ick noh de olle Fiskhütte gohn mag.“
sentences.l: When he is there, says he “o my gentlemen, give me but leave that I may go to the old fisher-hut.”
sentences.i: When he was there, he said: “O my gentlemen, grant me leave to go to the old fisherman’s hut.”
sentences.n: Es here is als, “when” — not es, “it.” gierwet = gebt (imperative plural); mie = mir; doh = doch, which makes the request pressing; Verlöv = Verlaub, Erlaubnis, leave; olle = alte; mag = möge. The last request of a condemned man is a fixed motif, and here it is the hinge of the tale.

sentences.t: Do tüt he sinen ollen Kiel an,
sentences.l: Then draws he his old smock on,
sentences.i: Then he put on his old smock,
sentences.n: “tüt … an” = zieht an, with the prefix an at the end (antrecken, anziehen). A Kiel is the coarse linen frock a fisherman or carter wore over his clothes. He arrived in the fine clothes of the enchanted castle; he changes into the one garment that can prove who he is.

sentences.t: do kümmet he wier noh de Heerens un seg „seih ji et nu wull, sin ick nig en armen Fisker sinen Sohn?
sentences.l: then comes he back to the gentlemen and says “do you see it now, am I not a poor fisherman’s son?
sentences.i: then he came back to the gentlemen and said: “Do you see it now — am I not a poor fisherman’s son?
sentences.n: “seih ji” = seht ihr; wull here is wohl, the particle pressing for agreement, not wull = wollte as elsewhere in this tale; “sin ick” = bin ich. “en armen Fisker sinen Sohn” is the construction the dialect loves and the schoolroom condemns: the possessor in the dative with a possessive after it — a poor fisherman his son — where the standard language says eines armen Fischers Sohn.

sentences.t: in düt Tueg heve ick minen Vader und Moder dat Braud gewunnen.“
sentences.l: in these clothes have I won the bread for my father and mother.”
sentences.i: In these clothes I earned the bread for my father and mother.”
sentences.n: düt = dies; Tueg is Zeug, here working clothes; heve = habe; minen = meinen; Braud = Brot; gewunnen = gewonnen. “das Brot gewinnen” is to earn one’s living. The source prints und here, in High German spelling, where the tale has un everywhere else — one of several places where the printer’s High German crosses the dialect.

sentences.t: Do erkennet se en un badden üm Vergiebnüs un niermt en met noh sin Hues,
sentences.l: Then recognise they him and begged for forgiveness and take him with them to his house,
sentences.i: Then they recognised him, and begged his pardon, and took him home with them to his house,
sentences.n: erkennet and niermt are present, badden past, all in one sentence — the tenses shift as a spoken telling shifts them. en here is ihn, “him,” where en elsewhere is ein, “a”; badden = baten; Vergiebnüs = Vergebung; “niermt … met” = nehmen mit; Hues = Haus. The town that would have hanged him for the word “fisherman” now begs his pardon.

sentences.t: do verteld he alle wü et em gohn hev, dat he wöre in en Wold kummen up en haujen Berg, do hädde sick de Berg updohn,
sentences.l: then told he all how it had gone with him, that he had come into a wood, up a high mountain, and the mountain had opened itself,
sentences.i: and then he told them everything that had befallen him: how he had come into a wood, up a high mountain, and the mountain had opened,
sentences.n: verteld = erzählte; wü = wie; “wü et em gohn hev” = wie es ihm gegangen hat. From here to the end of the retelling the verbs stand in the subjunctive — wöre, hädde, hädden — because he is reporting his own story; German marks reported speech this way and keeps it up for as long as the report lasts.

sentences.t: do wöre he in en verwünsket Schloß kummen, wo alles schwatt west wöre,
sentences.l: then he had come into an enchanted castle, where everything had been black,
sentences.i: and he had come into an enchanted castle where everything had been black,
sentences.n: “west wöre” = gewesen wäre. The retelling repeats the first account almost word for word — the tale tells things twice, as told tales do — and the small differences between the two tellings are the only thing to watch.

sentences.t: un drei Princessinnen wören der an kummen, de wören schwatt west, men en lück witt in’t Gesicht.
sentences.l: and three princesses had come there, they had been black, only a little white in the face.
sentences.i: and three princesses had come, and they had been black, only a little white in the face.
sentences.n: der is da, “there,” again; “an kummen” = angekommen. The little white in the face is repeated exactly as before: it is the one fact his mother will act on.

sentences.t: De hädden em segd he söll nig bange sien, he könn eer erlösen.
sentences.l: They had told him he should not be afraid, he could redeem them.
sentences.i: They had told him not to be afraid, and that he could set them free.
sentences.n: segd = gesagt, the past participle. What he leaves out of the retelling is the condition — the year of silence, the averted eyes — and that omission is what makes the advice he now gets possible.

sentences.t: Do seg sine Moder dat mög wull nig guet sien,
sentences.l: Then said his mother that might well not be good,
sentences.i: Then his mother said that might well not be a good thing,
sentences.n: mög = möge; wull here is wohl, “likely, surely”; guet = gut; Moder = Mutter. She is the only person in the tale who names the danger, and her remedy is the catastrophe.

sentences.t: he soll ’ne gewiehte Wasskeefze met niermen un drüppen (tropfen) eer gleinig (glühend) Wass in’t Gesicht.
sentences.l: he should take a consecrated wax-candle with him and drüppen (drip) their gleinig (glowing) wax into their faces.
sentences.i: he should take a consecrated wax candle with him and drip its burning wax into their faces.
sentences.n: Two more of the Grimms’ own parentheses in a single line: (tropfen) for drüppen and (glühend) for gleinig. gewiehte = geweihte, blessed; a Wasskeefze is a Wachskerze, a wax candle; eer here is ihr, “their.” Her reasoning is the ordinary reasoning of the folk tale — blessed wax against an enchantment. What it does is break the condition, and the tale does not soften what follows.

sentences.t: He geit wier hen un do gruelte (graute) em so,
sentences.l: He goes back again, and then it gruelte (dread came over) him so,
sentences.i: He went back again, and such dread came over him,
sentences.n: (graute) is the Grimms’ own gloss for the dialect gruelte: “es graute ihm,” he was seized with horror — an impersonal verb, with the person in the dative (em = ihm). This is grauen in the sense of dread, not the other grauen, of a grey day dawning.

sentences.t: un he drüppde er Wass in’t Gesicht, asse se sleipen, un se wören all halv witt.
sentences.l: and he dripped the wax into their faces, as they slept, and they were all half white.
sentences.n: er here is ihr, “their” — not er, “he,” which in this dialect is he. drüppde = tröpfelte; asse = als; sleipen = schliefen; all = alle. The wax works: they turn half white, which is to say half redeemed. It is the last thing in the tale that goes right.

sentences.t: Do sprüngen alle de drei Princessinnen up un segden „de verfluchte Hund, usse Bloet soll örfer die Rache schreien,
sentences.l: Then sprang all the three princesses up and said “the accursed dog, our blood shall cry vengeance upon you,
sentences.i: Then all three princesses sprang up and cried: “You accursed dog — our blood shall cry out for vengeance upon you,
sentences.n: die here is dich, “you” (accusative), not the article — this dialect writes di and die for dich, and does it again in the next line. örfer = über; usse = unser; Bloet = Blut. Blood crying for vengeance is the language of Genesis, where Abel’s blood cries out from the ground: the curse is deliberately biblical.

sentences.t: nu is kin Mensk up de Welt geboren un werd geboren, de us erlösen kann,
sentences.l: now is no person born on the earth, and none will be born, who can redeem us,
sentences.i: now there is no one born on this earth, nor will be born, who can set us free,
sentences.n: kin = kein; Mensk = Mensch. The two tenses side by side — is born and will be born — stretch the curse over all time. This is the turn of the tale: a redemption eight days from finished is now impossible for ever.

sentences.t: wie hevet noh drei Bröders, de sind in siewen Ketten anschloeten, de söllt die terreiten.“
sentences.l: we have yet three brothers, who are chained fast in seven chains: they shall tear you to pieces.”
sentences.i: we have three brothers still, bound fast in seven chains, and they shall tear you to pieces.”
sentences.n: wie here is wir, “we” — not wie, “how”; hevet = haben; noh = noch; Bröders = Brüder; siewen = sieben; anschloeten = angeschlossen, chained fast; söllt = sollen; die = dich again; terreiten = zerreißen. The three chained brothers are named here and never appear: the threat is not carried out, because the tale stops.

sentences.t: Do givt et en Gekriesk in’t ganse Schloß, un he sprank noh ut dat Fenster un terbrack dat Been,
sentences.l: Then there is a shrieking in the whole castle, and he yet sprang out of the window and broke the leg,
sentences.i: Then there was a shrieking through the whole castle, and he leapt out of the window even so, and broke his leg,
sentences.n: “givt et” = gibt es. A Gekriesk is a shrieking, a screeching — the ge- prefix makes a noun of continuous noise, as in Gekreisch. ganse = ganze; sprank = sprang; noh here is noch, “still, even so”; terbrack = zerbrach; “dat Been” = das Bein, and German says the leg where English says his leg.

sentences.t: un dat Schloß sunk wier in de Grunde, de Berg was wier to, un nümmes wust wo et west was.
sentences.l: and the castle sank again into the ground, the mountain was closed again, and nobody knew where it had been.
sentences.i: and the castle sank back into the ground, the mountain shut again, and nobody knew where it had stood.
sentences.n: sunk = sank; “was wier to” = war wieder zu, shut again; nümmes = niemand; wust = wußte (not willst); “wo et west was” = wo es gewesen war. The tale ends here, and it ends unresolved: the princesses are not redeemed, the brothers never come, the mountain shuts. The Grimms print it as a fragment, and nothing is known of any ending beyond this — an honest gap, not a lost page anyone can supply.

glossary.acht: acht — eight (the numeral; ‘in acht Dage’ = in acht Tagen)
glossary.aufgehoben: aufheben — lifted up, caught up and carried off (past part.; the Grimms’ own gloss for upnurmen)
glossary.bracht: Low German: gebracht — brought (bringen, past part.; ‘noh de Galge bracht’ = zum Galgen gebracht)
glossary.den: Low German: den — the (masc. sg.); this dialect uses den where High German has the dative dem (“von den Fiend” = von dem Feind)
glossary.der: Low German: da — there (‘do was der en armen Fisker’ = da war da ein armer Fischer; the article is de)
glossary.die: Low German: dich — you (accusative of du; the article is de)
glossary.eer: Low German: ihr — her, their; also sie — them (‘he könn eer erlösen’ = er könne sie erlösen)
glossary.en: Low German: ein — a, one; also = ihn, him (‘niermt en met’ = nehmen ihn mit)
glossary.er: Low German: ihr — their (possessive; ‘er Wass’ = ihr Wachs)
glossary.ersten: Low German: erst — first, beforehand (adverbial; ‘he wull ersten … hebben’ = er wollte erst … haben)
glossary.es: Low German: als — as, when (‘Es he do is’ = als er da ist)
glossary.gans: Low German: ganz — quite, whole, entirely (not die Gans, the goose)
glossary.graute: grauen — dreaded, was filled with horror (impersonal, es graute ihm; the Grimms’ own gloss for gruelte)
glossary.heer: Low German: Herr — Mister, sir, lord (‘Heer Börgemester’ = Herr Bürgermeister; pl. Heerens)
glossary.je: Low German: ja — yes (‘do seg he je’ = da sagte er ja)
glossary.könn: Low German: könne — could, might (können, 3rd sg. subjunctive of reported speech)
glossary.leiten: Low German: ließen — let, had (something) done (laten = lassen, 3rd pl. past; ‘leiten se dat ut trummen’ = ließen sie es austrommeln)
glossary.noh: Low German: nach — to, toward; also = noch, still, yet (“noh drei Bröders” = noch drei Brüder; “sprank noh ut dat Fenster” = sprang noch aus dem Fenster)
glossary.richtet: richten — executed, put to death (past part. gerichtet; ‘an de Galge richtet weren’ = am Galgen gerichtet werden)
glossary.seg: Low German: sagte, sagt — said, says (seggen = sagen; ‘do seg he’ = da sagte er)
glossary.segd: Low German: gesagt — said (seggen = sagen, past part.)
glossary.sin: Low German: sein — his; also bin, seid — am, are (‘sin ick nig …?’ = bin ich nicht …?; ‘wo sin ji’ = wie seid ihr)
glossary.t: Low German: ’t = dat — the (the reduced article; “in’t Gesicht” = in das Gesicht, ins Gesicht); elsewhere ’t = et, ‘it’
glossary.tropfen: tropfen — to drip, to let fall in drops (the Grimms’ own gloss for drüppen); not der Tropfen, a drop
glossary.was: Low German: war — was (sein, 3rd sg. past; the dialect word for ‘what’ is wat)
glossary.well: Low German: wer — whoever (‘well de schaffen könne’ = wer die schaffen könnte); not will
glossary.wie: Low German: wir — we (‘wie hevet’ = wir haben)
glossary.willt: Low German: will — wants, will (wollen, 3rd sg.)
glossary.wo: Low German: wo — where; in this dialect also = wie, how
glossary.wull: Low German: wollte — wanted; also = wohl, surely (‘seih ji et nu wull’, ‘dat mög wull nig guet sien’)
glossary.wören: Low German: waren — were (sein, 3rd pl. past); in the retelling wären, the past subjunctive of reported speech
